answers.body:
If we have incomplete information, we can regret a perfectly rational decision’s outcome or the decision itself.

For example, after the fact, we could see that "Even though Choice A was the most rational given what I knew, Choice B would have provided me more utility given how things actually turned out.".

Now, if I could have learned more information that would have led to Choice B but I didn’t look for it (knowingly or not) then I will regret my actual decision, not because it wasn’t rational given the information I had but because I didn’t use all the information that was available to me.

————————————-

In decision theory, you can try to "minimize max regret" as an objective -- in which case you want to minimize the maximum difference between the outcome you get and the outcome you would have gotten had you known everything.

With regards to the distinction between "making a choice" (taking the action represented by a choice or option) and "deciding to make a choice" (making a commitment to perform the action represented by a choice):

Are the remarks in parentheses your own interpretation? I ask because it made me think of decision making in cases where there is an ethical dilemma like the trolley problem. Suppose that one could save four people by pulling a lever in order to change the course of a trolley which would mean the death of four people, to a course which would mean death for one person. Some people would rather not take a decision in this case. Rather than to take responsibility they would let fate decide. Not doing anything relieves them (or so they feel) from moral responsibility.

To answer your question, in some cases regret is unavoidable. Even if one were to decide rationally to save four people, one would still feel morally responsible for the death of that one person. I guess this is why some people prefer not to do anything.

Caveat: I'm not a logician, so my understanding is offered in lieu of the more "speculative" responses from the various creative thinkers.

You ask:

Can a rational decision ever be regretted?

and later:

Or are there particular (types of) scenarios in which even for an ideal rational agent it is possible to come to regret their choice?

According to some causal decision theorists, yes. From Causal Decision Theory (SEP):

In response to Egan, Frank Arntzenius (2008) and Joyce (2012) argue that in some decision problems an agent’s rational deliberations using freely available information do not settle on a single option but instead settle on a probability distribution over options. They acknowledge that the agent may regret the option issuing from these deliberations but differ about the regret’s significance. Arntzenius holds that the regret counts against the option’s rationality, whereas Joyce denies this.

It is clear from the passage that the nature of regret in this context is controversial.

You also say:

to my surprise that some authors make a distinction between "making a choice" (taking the action represented by a choice or option) and "deciding to make a choice" (making a commitment to perform the action represented by a choice). I don't quite understand why it would ever be necessary to make that distinction (I never saw it being made in game theory for instance), but if one does make this, then there does seem to be a way how even in an idealized model regret might sneak in, namely, if somehow by committing oneself to a choice (after deliberation, and "rationally" selecting the "best" possible choice), the situation changes so that one would (immediately) regret actually going through with it and performing the associated action. But is that really possible?

From the same article:

Decision theory underlies game theory because a game’s solution identifies rational choices in the decision problems the game creates for the players. Solutions to games distinguish correlation and causation, as do decision principles

Let's understand CDT for what it is. It is an attempt to understand how causal understanding to utilitarian ends functions under bounded rationality and differs from rather evidential understanding based on Bayesian theory by understanding that one's causal model has a direct impact on one's probabilistic model. Making a choice, then is believing that the current Bayesian theory is adequate for predicting future events, where as deciding to make a choice is understanding that future events affect priors in making a choice and seeking to use causality to model the most likely theory of the most likely (as I understand it). That is Bayesian theory is atemporal in the sense that it is calculated presuming the priors are fixed (necessarily so), where as CDT knows that cause and effect over time affect priors. From Bayesian Decision Theory (lesswrong.com):

From the perspective of Bayesian decision theory, any kind of probability distribution - such as the distribution for tomorrow's weather - represents a prior distribution. That is, it represents how we expect today the weather is going to be tomorrow. This contrasts with frequentist inference, the classical probability interpretation, where conclusions about an experiment are drawn from a set of repetitions of such experience, each producing statistically independent results... Suppose we intend to meet a friend tomorrow, and expect an 0.5 chance of raining. If we are choosing between various options for the meeting, with the pleasantness of some of the options (such as going to the park) being affected by the possibility of rain, we can assign values to the different options with or without rain. We can then pick the option whose expected value is the highest, given the probability of rain.

Therefore, when one commits oneself to a model of probability one is making a choice, but when one commits oneself to a causal model, one is tentatively selecting the model, and as new causes and effects unravel, one can see that a gulf between one's old model of probability and the current state of affairs that said model has now diverged from no longer maximizes utility. It is the deviation of model from the external world that causes grief called regret.

As an aside, my wife bets on the NFL by betting on players scoring by the end of the game. She uses her subjective probabilities. Then early in the game, some change up in the opposing team's lineup, for instance, the introduction of a different type of defense strategy based on a player going onto the injury roster affects who is put on the field. That then impacts her subjective probabilities. But being locked into the bet after a certain point, she experiences regret because psychologically, her causal model has updated causing her subjective probabilities to change, but she is unable to reallocate her choice. Thus, she decided to make a choice, and until she was locked in, she in a way hadn't made the choice because she could change her choice based on events prior to lock in.

Of course, as wife the same will tell you, I might have made everything in this response up.

Usually one would say from their daily life, "A rational decision sometimes leads to regret. Similarly, an irrational decision sometimes leads to happiness."

There may be many unfortunate men who have had to listen to the accusations of others even for their rational decisions. So, one can jokingly say that it depends on the reaction of the other person, or creature.

If a person is completely confident in the rational decision he made, it is less likely to be regretted. In such cases, it depends on the attitude of the person who made the rational decision.

While a rational decision is made, if one considers the possible reaction, severity, area affected, duration, etc., it is less likely to lead to regret. If one focuses on a specific person or thing instead of considering a larger area, population, duration, etc., it can often lead to regret.

Sometimes, a decision made at a particular moment may seem entirely rational. However, upon receiving further information, one might well feel that a new rational decision could have been made a bit later. This often happens in our lives. Yet, at the very moment the decision is made, we typically do not feel any regret about it. If the new information comes from sources other than one's own memory, that subsequent regret cannot be attributed to the decision having been rational.

Had more factors been considered in order of priority when making a rational decision, no one could have said that one would later regret it.

So, IMHO, a rational decision cannot be considered rational if it is a cause of regret. If a rational decision leaves regret, consider it as a disaster or a mishap occurred due to some reason for the time being.

Can a rational decision ever be regretted?

This depends on your point of view. I'd argue that regret doesn't come from the decision process unless that process is found to be flawed. Regret comes from the consequences of an action and this is particularly true when the consequences are unexpected and undesirable.

I am reading up on causal decision theory, and saw to my surprise that some authors make a distinction between "making a choice" (taking the action represented by a choice or option) and "deciding to make a choice" (making a commitment to perform the action represented by a choice). I don't quite understand why it would ever be necessary to make that distinction.

There is a difference between decision and action. For a proper analysis of an event, both are required since a rational and proper decision may lead to an action with undesired consequences.

Conversely, a poor decision can lead to no adverse consequences. Many people have driven after consuming too much alcohol and haven't hurt anyone while driving. These persons feel no regret until their action leads to an accident.

Definitely

There are elements of randomness to life, or at least elements that would appear to be random to any human. It is therefore possible and even I would say common for even the most rational decisions to risk regret. Even with all possible information at a given moment, the results may be regrettable.

For a simple example, say I'm offered a chance to bet on a single roll of a 10-sided die, but it's a one time offer. For a payment of $10.00, I will get a payoff of $100.00 on any roll number other than a 1. The expected value of this bet is $90 (the odds of a payout multiplied by the value of the payout, setting aside the cost). It is entirely rational to pay $10 to get something with an expected value of $90. But if I make the bet and lose, I may well regret doing it even though it was obviously rational.

Also, there are situations were every path leads to regret. There are times when you are picking the least bad option where there are no good options.

Imagine your loving spouse and a good friend are both in danger and you are able to save exactly one of them. Note that situation explicitly assumes you love your spouse. Most people will probably chose their spouse and barring certain edge cases that is probably the most rational choice both emotionally and from a purely practical standpoint. But it almost doesn't matter. You will likely regret whatever choice you make for the rest of your life. You may never once doubt or waiver that you were right. You might be able to make charts showing that for you your choice was clearly the most rational and possibly also the most ethically correct. But you will almost certainly still have feelings of regret for the rest of your life. There was no good decision, only an opportunity to take the lesser of two evils.

One of the problems with the rational decision model you're referencing (and there are many, so don't take this as my sole critique) is that it assumes preferences are dimensionless. Even if we assume a perfectly rational, perfectly informed, perfectly self-aware agent, the agent will necessarily change over time, meaning that 'perfect' decisions at a given time will not remain perfect accord with the agent's ever-changing self.

As the oil French saying goes, someone who isn't a rebel in their 20s has no heart, but someone who's still a rebel in their 40s has no brain…

Caveat: the answer ("yes") seems so straightforward to me, that I'm probably missing something. Also not a professional philosopher.

An easy example for when you would regret a rational decision is this:

  • You make a bet on a roll of 10 dice - if you get a perfect 6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6, you lose your money. In every other case, you gain 100 times of what you put in.
  • Assume you have perfect information about everything including the fact that no cheating is going on, the dice are true (i.e., perfectly random) and you know about yourself that having plenty of money makes you happier. You also know about yourself that you are not having a hidden agenda of becoming a monk, unburdened by possessions. You also have a good understanding about the maths of probabilities, expected values and so on.
  • The only information you do not have beforehand is the result of the roll. If you had that information, then it would not be a decision at all, arguably.

After carefully calculating your expected value, you bet all your money including your house and life savings and the savings you put away for your children. The dice are rolled, and 6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6-6 turns up. You lose all your money and end up in poverty until death.

Now I have no scientific proof, but I can suspect that a great many people would indeed feel regret. Your error during the decision-making was that while you correctly calculated the expected value of your decision, you failed to take into account that while the bad outcome was very very unlikely, it was still possible. This would have been a completely normal human fallacy (the inverse of which happens every day for people who play in a lottery).

NB: If you say that your scenario requires that this kind of error can not happen, then it's not a decision at all - then it's just an algorithm you're running, completely predetermined. If you chose the algorithm, then you can of course again regret possibly choosing the wrong algorithm. If you argue that the algorithm is "built-in" in the decider with no choice, then you end up at the full non-free-will scenario, and there can be no regret in that case.

NB2: Every decision, rational or not, requires that you don't know the future (otherwise it's not a decision). Not knowing the future means that bad results are possible (if only good results are possible, you might still call it a decision, but it would just be an inconsequential one). So if something is a real decision, then regret is always possible, no matter how much information or decision-making skills you possess.

Also, prompted by a comment, note that there seems to be a difference between regret and remorse in the english language:

Regret differs from remorse in that people can regret things beyond their control, but remorse indicates a sense of responsibility for the situation.

By that statement, even if you are a completely rational decision maker, and aware of it, you may still regret the outcome of your decision (i.e., regret that the dice fell as they did, here). The decision was in your control, the dice weren't. You could reasonably even regret ever being put in the position to have to make the decision.

Yes, rational decisions can be regretted, because reason is not necessary logical (reason is the mechanism of thinking, and, when we think, we all break logic constantly; if not, we would be LITERALLY PERFECT entities).

LOGICAL decisions cannot be regretted, since they...

a) are simple and

b) imply necessity (2+2=4 is necessary, no place for regret).

On the contrary, RATIONAL decisions can be regretted since they ...

a) are complex (they are based on large numbers of facts to consider; for example, deciding to go to the movies implies financial, economic, biological, social, commercial, religious, ideological, (... etc.) considerations). Complexity involves doubt, doubt leads to error, and error implies regret.

b) imply contingency (the act of drinking poison can be good or bad, depending on the amount of poison; some types of poison are known to be good when taken in small doses). Contingency makes decisions largely complex to take, increasing the probability of destructive outcomes, and so, regret.

An "ideal rational agent" would think in a perfect and consistent logic (it would never ever be wrong), so, it would be a literally perfect entity, which is not possible.

Since regret is part of the mechanism of learning, then,

... an absolute lack of regret would imply an absolute knowledge of nature.

Such is way far from being human.

Several answers have already talked about how you can make rational probabilistic decisions, get unlucky, and regret being unlucky. I think this isn't regretting your decision, per se, so much as regretting your bad luck. Similarly when choosing rationally between two bad alternatives, I think your regret is best understood as regretting being put into that situation, rather than regretting the particular choice you made.

I think it's more interesting to ask whether you can regret decisions ex ante: that is, your decision theory tells you to do X and not Y, while your world model tells you that doing X is worse for you than doing Y. As I see it, the point of decision theory design is to avoid doing this, but the common decision theories that I know about either have known cases where they do something like this, or are underspecified / not obviously implementable in practice.

Examples where a common decision theory gets arguably the wrong answer:

  • Newcomb's problem
  • Smoking lesion
  • Parfit's hitch-hiker

In all these cases I think we have an ideal of what properties we would expect of our choices and actions to call them "rational", and we have some attempts to specify how to make choices and which actions to take in order to be "rational", and it seems like the specifications fall short of achieving the properties. Whether you choose to describe this as "you can act rationally and still regret your choice" or "we don't actually know how to act rationally, even in principle, even given all relevant information" is, I think, up to you.

The classical tragedy puts its protagonists in situations which cannot have a good ending. No matter what choice the protagonist makes, tragedy ensues. Invariably, there would be regret.

Another, somewhat related general argument is that individuals are not monolithic. Norbert Elias emphasizes in his The Civilizing Process how the mind of a person is not a static, layered structure of id/ego/super-ego but instead a dynamically interacting assembly of mental agents with their own agenda. Invariably, many decisions we make do not satisfy all of these often conflicting agendas. As an example, faced with the choice of betraying one's spouse with an extremely attractive specimen of the desired sex may invariably result in regret — different regret depending on the choice we make, but regret nonetheless; even if we make the best-informed decision with complete self-knowledge (an obvious fiction already) it is impossible to avoid regret.

Let me tell you about Daniel, a successful investment banker who learned this the hard way.

Daniel had spent years building his career, earning a reputation as one of the sharpest minds in the finance world. One day, an opportunity landed on his desk—a struggling company that needed his expertise to survive. Daniel came up with a plan that was bold and, to most people, brilliant. He found ways to restructure their debt, exploit a few tax loopholes, and make the company look much healthier than it really was. Everything he did was technically legal, but ethically? Let’s just say there was a gray area.

The plan worked. Investors were thrilled, the company rebounded, and Daniel’s cut of the deal was enormous. Flush with cash, he started buying up real estate, setting up offshore accounts, and dreaming of early retirement. He told himself, "I’ve earned this. I’ll retire by 45, buy a yacht, and spend the rest of my life living it up."

From a business perspective, every decision Daniel made seemed perfectly logical. But there was one thing he didn’t account for: his life was not his own to control. That very night, Daniel suffered a sudden stroke and died.

As his family and business partners scrambled to untangle his financial web, Daniel found himself standing before God. All the wealth and success he’d worked so hard to build were meaningless now. The words of Jesus rang true: "You fool! This very night your life will be demanded from you. Then who will get what you have prepared for yourself?" (Luke 12:20).

中文：

我認為，後悔發生在選擇之後。

當我們做出選擇的那一刻，選擇就已經完成了。它不能再被改變，也不能回到選擇發生以前的狀態。

但我認為，後悔並不是沒有意義的。

後悔可以成為讓下一次選擇變得更清楚的一個轉換點。這也是人類成長最基本的收穫之一。

這一次的選擇可能沒有得到你想要的結果，所以你後悔了。但你已經不能改變這一次的選擇，你能做的是把這一次的經驗帶到下一次。

因此，下一次的選擇會因為這一次的後悔，而變得更加清楚，也更加接近你真正想要的方向。

所以我不認為，後悔必然代表原本的決策是不理性的。

一個決策可以在當時是理性的，而在之後仍然被後悔。因為後悔不是重新做一次之前的選擇，而是讓已經完成的選擇成為下一次選擇的一部分。

English:

I think regret occurs after a choice has been made.

At the moment we make a choice, the choice is already complete. It cannot be changed anymore, and we cannot return to the state we were in before the choice was made.

But I do not think regret is therefore meaningless.

On the contrary, I think Regret can become a turning point that makes the next choice clearer. It is also one of the most basic ways in which human beings grow.

Perhaps the choice did not produce the outcome we wanted, and that is why we regret it. But we cannot change that choice anymore. What we can do is carry the experience of that choice into the next one.

Because of that regret, the next choice can become clearer and more firmly directed toward what we actually want.

So I do not think that regret necessarily means that the original decision was irrational.

A decision can be rational at the time it is made and still be regretted later. Regret is not a way of making the previous choice again. It is a way of allowing a completed choice to become part of the next one.

items.title: Can a rational decision ever be regretted?
items.body:
In "real life" we often make decisions under time pressure, without all the information we would want, without full knowledge about the consequences of our actions, and even without always being totally clear about what we desire or prefer. Even when we then make "rational" decisions, that is, try to be as prudent as possible and take every relevant piece of information into account, those decisions may later easily turn out to be regrettable. Our beliefs may turn out to have been wrong, or something unforeseen may happen, or it may turn out that our actual preferences were different from what we thought. (The grass is always greener on the other side.) So, in this sense rational decisions can easily be regretted later.

However, in normative decision theory a model of ideal rationality is developed. You might think that an ideal rational agent (who has perfect self-knowledge, whose preferences are simply "given", and who has all the relevant information) can never come to regret their choices. Is that so? Or are there particular (types of) scenarios in which even for an ideal rational agent it is possible to come to regret their choice?

Background: I am reading up on causal decision theory, and saw to my surprise that some authors make a distinction between "making a choice" (taking the action represented by a choice or option) and "deciding to make a choice" (making a commitment to perform the action represented by a choice). I don't quite understand why it would ever be necessary to make that distinction (I never saw it being made in game theory for instance), but if one does make this, then there does seem to be a way how even in an idealized model regret might sneak in, namely, if somehow by committing oneself to a choice (after deliberation, and "rationally" selecting the "best" possible choice), the situation changes so that one would (immediately) regret actually going through with it and performing the associated action. But is that really possible? Are there causal decision theorists who hold that this kind of situation actually occurs (without assuming change of the agent's preferences or desires)? If so, are there more or less realistic examples of those kind of scenarios?
